question: A Patient who is on antihypertensive drug develops a dry cough. Which of the following drug might be responsible for the condition:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "ACE inhibitors" -> "inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme" -> "accumulation of bradykinin in the respiratory tract" -> "irritation of respiratory tract" -> "dry cough" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Diuretics" -> "alteration of fluid and electrolyte balance" -> "no direct effect on respiratory tract" -> "unlikely to cause dry cough" -> 10%
CHAIN: "Calcium channel blockers" -> "blockage of calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle" -> "no direct effect on respiratory tract" -> "unlikely to cause dry cough" -> 10%
CHAIN: "Beta blockers" -> "blockade of beta-adrenergic receptors" -> "possible mild respiratory symptoms" -> "dry cough is rare" -> 20%
analysis: The core medical principle in this scenario involves understanding the side effects associated with different classes of antihypertensive drugs. Among the options provided, ACE inhibitors are well-documented to cause a dry cough as a side effect. This is attributed to the accumulation of bradykinin in the respiratory tract, which occurs due to the inhibition of the enzyme peptidyl-dipeptidase A (also known as angiotensin-converting enzyme). This side effect is a recognized and common reason for patients discontinuing ACE inhibitors. The other drug classes listed, such as diuretics, calcium channel blockers, and beta blockers, do not typically cause dry cough as a direct side effect of their mechanisms of action. Therefore, based on medical consensus and the biochemical pathway involved, ACE inhibitors are the most likely cause of the dry cough in this patient.
